title: Is Occidental Petroleum Still a Buy Now that WTI's Down to $70 a Barrel? - The Globe and Mail
content: Oxy is more exposed to volatile crude oil prices than larger integrated oil and gas giants. But oil remains far above its breakeven levels for supporting its capex and dividends. Occidental Petroleum(NYSE: OXY), the oil and gas giant more commonly known as Oxy, hit a 52-week high of $67.45 per share on March 31. That year-to-date gain of nearly 60% was largely driven by the Middle East conflict's impact on oil prices. But as of this writing, Oxy's stock trades at about $50. It pulled back as WTI crude oil prices retreated from a four-year high of $112.25 per barrel in mid-May to around $70. Let's see why Oxy's stock is tightly tethered to crude oil prices -- and if it's still worth buying today. Where to invest $1,000 right now? Our analyst team just revealed what they believe are the 10 best stocks to buy right now, when you join Stock Advisor. See the stocks » Oxy is less diversified than integrated energy giants like ExxonMobil(NYSE: XOM) and Chevron(NYSE: CVX). While ExxonMobil and Chevron operate a diverse mix of upstream, midstream, and downstream businesses, Oxy generates most of its revenue from its upstream business -- which handles the exploration, drilling, and extraction of oil and natural gas. A smaller percentage of Oxy's revenue comes from its midstream business, which operates oil and gas pipelines. A small but growing sliver of its top line comes from its low-carbon ventures business, which develops carbon capture and direct air capture technologies. Generally speaking, rising oil prices provide the strongest tailwinds for upstream companies, as their revenue growth will easily outpace operating expenses. But when oil prices decline, their expenses can rise faster than their revenues. So when crude oil prices surged earlier this year, Oxy's stock outperformed ExxonMobil and Chevron. However, Oxy underperformed both energy giants over the past month after a ceasefire and peace talks between the U.S. and Iran reduced crude oil prices. To sustain its current capital expenditures and dividends, Oxy needs oil to remain above $40- $45 per barrel. Its free cash flow also significantly increases at above $60 per barrel. WTI was below $60 per barrel throughout most of 2025 and early 2026, but it hasn't fallen below $45 since the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. Therefore, Oxy's profits should continue rising unless a global recession triggers another historical collapse in oil demand. Oxy's stock still looks cheap at 10 times forward earnings, but that multiple could rise if analysts lower their near-term forecasts to reflect declining oil prices. That said, its business is broadly stable, and it's taken major steps to reduce its debt from its poorly timed $55 billion acquisition of Anadarko in 2019. It's a safe oil stock to hold right now, but I'd prefer to invest in more diversified energy plays like ExxonMobil and Chevron in this choppy market. The United States-Iran roadmap reduced concern around conflict-driven disruption. That helped push crude lower and changed the tone across energy names. For ExxonMobil, the event highlighted how external forces can shape market performance even when company operations remain unchanged. This is a core feature of the oil and gas sector. Commodity prices respond to global developments, and large energy companies often move with those signals. ExxonMobil’s size remains one of its defining features. The company has the ability to manage large projects, operate complex refineries, maintain global supply networks, and support technology development across its business lines. Scale also helps the company compete with other global energy producers, national oil companies, refiners, and petrochemical firms. Its integrated structure allows it to participate across exploration, production, refining, marketing, and chemicals. That breadth can support stability through changing commodity conditions. However, the business still remains tied to energy prices, demand trends, and operating costs. Traditional oil and gas companies face changing regulation, shifting consumption patterns, and rising attention on lower-carbon energy systems. At the same time, crude, natural gas, fuels, and petrochemicals remain deeply embedded in transportation, manufacturing, and industrial activity. ExxonMobil continues operating within this complex environment. Its business must address current energy needs while adapting to longer-term changes across global markets. That balance remains a major theme for integrated energy companies. ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM), latest pressure came from a broader crude market move rather than a company-specific operational shock. The de-escalation roadmap between the United States and Iran cooled oil prices and weighed on the wider energy group. For ExxonMobil, the move highlighted upstream sensitivity while also reminding the market of the company’s diversified business structure. Its refining, marketing, and chemicals segments add depth, while its upstream portfolio keeps it closely linked to crude pricing. The company remains one of the most visible names in the oil and gas sector whenever energy prices move sharply. content: Enbridge has increased its dividend for 31 straight years. ExxonMobil expects to grow its earnings and cash flow at double-digit rates through 2030, with new businesses driving additional growth into the 2040s. NextEra Energy's deal for Dominion Energy will accelerate earnings growth to 9%+ over the next decade. The global economy is always adapting and evolving. As a result, companies need to remain innovative to stay ahead. Some companies have done an excellent job at keeping up with the times over the years, enabling them to grow their earnings and dividends for decades. Enbridge(NYSE: ENB), ExxonMobil(NYSE: XOM), and NextEra Energy(NYSE: NEE) stand out for their dividend growth records. These energy companies have increased their payouts each year for more than three decades, which should continue for at least the next 10 years despite the sector's shift toward cleaner energy. That makes them ideal dividend stocks to buy and hold for the next decade. Where to invest $1,000 right now? Our analyst team just revealed what they believe are the 10 best stocks to buy right now, when you join Stock Advisor. See the stocks » A decade ago, Enbridge got nearly three-quarters of its earnings from its oil and liquids pipeline segment, with the rest from lower-carbon energy (gas and renewable power). Today, more than half its earnings come from lower-carbon energy. Enbridge has invested heavily to grow its cleaner energy platforms through acquisitions and organic expansion projects. The Canadian pipeline and utility company's shift to lower-carbon energy should continue in the coming decade. Enbridge ended the first quarter with 40 billion Canadian dollars ($28 billion) of secured growth capital projects in the backlog, which should enter service by the early 2030s. While its projects span liquids, gas, and renewables, the bulk of its spending is on cleaner energy. Meanwhile, it's pursuing about CA$50 billion ($35 billion) in additional growth capital projects, which it could approve by 2030, primarily in gas and renewables. These projects should support about 5% annual cash flow per share growth after this year. That will give Enbridge the fuel to continue increasing its more than 5%-yielding dividend in the coming decade. The company has now raised its payout for 31 consecutive years (in Canadian dollars). ExxonMobil's current focus is on becoming an even more profitable oil and gas producer. It's investing heavily to develop its advantaged resources (lowest cost and highest margins) while also executing a multi-year structural cost-savings program. This strategy should grow its earnings capacity by $25 billion and cash flow by $35 billion by 2030, at the same margins and prices as in 2024. That's double-digit annual growth rates. The oil giant's plan would enable it to produce $145 billion in surplus cash during that period at $65 oil. That would give Exxon the funds to continue increasing its 3%-yielding dividend, which it has done for 43 consecutive years. While Exxon's main focus is on producing oil and gas, the energy giant is also ramping up its investments in the energy sources we'll need in the future. It's developing carbon capture and storage, lithium, and biofuels projects. Additionally, Exxon is investing in new businesses, including Proxxima (polyolefin thermoset resin systems that outperform epoxy and polyurethane) and carbon materials. These businesses have the potential to reach $13 billion in earnings by 2040, while driving Exxon's growth for decades. NextEra Energy owns the country's largest electric utility and is a leading clean energy development company. It has invested heavily in renewable energy over the years, driving robust growth. NextEra has increased its nearly 3%-yielding dividend for more than 30 consecutive years, including delivering double-digit compound annual dividend growth over the last two decades. The company currently expects to invest between $295 billion and $325 billion in capex through 2032 to support surging U.S. power demand. That should give NextEra Energy the power to grow its adjusted earnings per share at a compound annual rate of more than 8% through 2032, with it highly likely to continue growing at that rate through at least 2035. That should support continued dividend increases, with NextEra targeting 6% compound annual growth in 2027 and 2028. NextEra Energy recently pounced on the opportunity to accelerate its growth by agreeing to acquire Dominion Energy. The deal will create the world's largest regulated electric utility business and boost its growth rate to more than 9% annually through 2032, a rate it believes it can extend through 2035. The larger-scale company will be able to operate more efficiently, putting it in an even stronger position to capitalize on the AI power boom. As a result, it should have plenty of power to continue increasing its dividend in the decade ahead. Exxon, Enbridge, and NextEra Energy have already increased their dividends every year for decades. That upward trend should continue over the coming decade as they support the world's growing energy needs. Their combinations of higher yields and visible growth make them ideal dividend stocks to buy and hold for the next 10 years. title: Exxon Saves Billions, But Margins Still Cut In Half - Trefis
content:
Management once built its transformation story on massive cost discipline — and it’s still telling it, louder than ever. Yet as profit margins fall by nearly half, a harder question emerges: if record cost savings can’t hold the line, how resilient is the “transformed” company really? Listen to Exxon Mobil (XOM) today, and you’ll hear a story of operational might. The company is rightly proud of hitting “record levels of production in Guyana,” boosting refinery throughput, and leveraging its global scale to navigate a world in conflict. It’s a compelling story about producing more. But the operational story isn’t the one that should hold your attention. Beneath the record barrels sits a harder fact: ExxonMobil is cutting more structural costs than ever, and its margins are still compressing. The efficiency engine that was supposed to make the company cycle-proof is running at full tilt, yet profitability has nearly halved. That gap is the story. The Cost Story Is Still Growing, So Why Aren’t Margins? Management’s transformation case has long been anchored in one number: cumulative structural cost taken out of the business since 2019. That figure hasn’t gone quiet: it has gotten bigger. It stood at $12.7 billion as of early 2025, and by the first quarter of 2026 had reached $15.6 billion, with management reaffirming a $20 billion target by 2030. Far from abandoning the efficiency narrative, Exxon is still leading with it. That’s exactly what makes the margin picture so striking. The cost-out program is delivering on plan, and the company is still posting record volumes, yet the bottom line tells a different story. The new center of gravity is clear: volume. Management now leads with operational metrics that show its scale and responsiveness. You hear about how “refinery throughput increased by approximately 200,000 barrels a day” in a single month and how, excluding external disruptions, underlying “upstream production was up 8%” year-over-year. The narrative has migrated from the bottom line back to the top line, from durable efficiency to immediate output. But the profitability behind those barrels has thinned. ExxonMobil’s trailing-twelve-month net margin peaked near 15% in early 2023, and now net margin sits at 7.8% as of the first quarter of 2026, close to half. The cost savings are real and still compounding; they simply haven’t been enough to offset weaker crude realizations, higher depreciation, and Middle East-driven disruption. Here’s the concern: if structural savings still can’t hold the line on margins, it suggests the easy, durable efficiency gains may be doing less of the heavy lifting than the “transformed company” narrative implied. As analyzed in The Number That Could Test Exxon Mobil Stock, the first real test, a softer price-and-margin environment compounded by geopolitical disruption, shows that cost discipline alone isn’t fully absorbing the hit. The key metric to watch next quarter is simple: net margin. If it stabilizes as the $20 billion savings program advances, the resilience case holds. If it keeps eroding while cost-out keeps climbing, the question becomes uncomfortable: how much more can efficiency offset before price does the talking? This is the kind of subtle change that is easy to miss in a flood of production numbers. The headline metrics still impress, but the economics underneath them have moved. Exxon Mobil has quietly become a different bet than the one many investors thought they owned; not because the cost story disappeared, but because it’s no longer enough to keep margins where they were. Every stock you own is shifting shape the same way Exxon Mobil is, and the only way to stay aligned is to keep asking where the value really sits now versus when you bought in. title: ExxonMobil Announces Planned Effective Date for Move to Texas - Exxon Mobil Corporation
content:
SPRING, Texas--(BUSINESS WIRE)--
Exxon Mobil Corporation today announced that its redomiciliation from New Jersey to Texas is expected to become effective on July 1, 2026. As part of this change, ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation will become the publicly traded parent company, replacing Exxon Mobil Corporation of New Jersey. Shares will continue to trade on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker symbol “XOM,” and shareholders are not required to take any action. Shareholders approved the move to Texas at the company’s 2026 Annual Meeting. Additional details are available in the company’s filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. ExxonMobil expects to file a Form 8-K upon completion. ExxonMobil, one of the largest publicly traded international energy and petrochemical companies, creates solutions that improve quality of life and meet society’s evolving needs. The Company’s primary businesses - Upstream, Product Solutions and Low Carbon Solutions – provide products that enable modern life, including energy, chemicals, lubricants, and lower emissions technologies. ExxonMobil holds an industry-leading portfolio of resources, and is one of the largest integrated fuels, lubricants, and chemical companies in the world. ExxonMobil also owns and operates the largest CO2 pipeline network in the United States. In 2021, ExxonMobil announced Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emission-reduction plans for 2030 for operated assets, compared to 2016 levels. The plans are to achieve a 20-30% reduction in corporate-wide greenhouse gas intensity; a 40-50% reduction in greenhouse gas intensity of upstream operations; a 70-80% reduction in corporate-wide methane intensity; and a 60-70% reduction in corporate-wide flaring intensity. To learn more, visit exxonmobil.com and ExxonMobil’s Advancing Climate Solutions. title: What a Market Shock Does to Exxon Mobil Stock - Trefis
content:
A steep fall and a long wait to recover are the risks you carry in this energy giant. Exxon Mobil (XOM) stock’s 2.1% drop in the latest session caps a month that has seen it fall 15.2%. As an integrated oil and gas giant, the company is delivering strong operational results, with management highlighting record production in Guyana and progress in the Permian on its latest call. Yet the market is also weighing significant disruption, particularly to key LNG assets in the Middle East that face a multi-year repair timeline. This brings a critical question into focus for any shareholder. That question isn’t about the day-to-day. It’s about what happens in a true market crisis. When the entire market sells off, how far does a stock like this fall, how long does it stay down, and can you, as an owner, ride that out? History provides a clear, unvarnished picture of the risk. Across the 15 major market shocks it has traded through, Exxon Mobil stock fell an average of 15% from peak to trough, which is roughly in line with the S&P 500’s average 16% decline in those same periods. But the worst case is what you need to internalize. The stock’s single deepest drawdown was 48%, which occurred during the 2020 COVID-19 Crash. The environment where it has been hit hardest is what analysts call a “Growth & Demand Scare.” That category includes real, memorable events like the 2015-2016 China devaluation scare, the sharp Q4 2018 selloff, and the COVID crash. Surviving the fall is one thing; enduring the recovery is another. For the shocks it has fully recovered from, it has taken a median of about 6 months for the stock to climb back to its pre-shock high. However, the wait can be much longer. After the 2008-2009 Global Financial Crisis, shareholders were underwater for about 44 months before the stock reclaimed its prior peak. A swift recovery in the past is not a promise for the future. [5] 2013 Taper Tantrum: Bernanke’s taper hint spiked Treasury yields, triggering emerging market capital flight.

[10] 2020 COVID-19 Crash: Pandemic lockdowns caused history’s fastest bear market before massive stimulus drove recovery.

The Beaumont refinery expansion, completed in 2023, has already recovered its initial investment. These are signs of a robust and profitable operation. However, the company also faces new, specific headwinds. On its latest earnings call, management confirmed that damaged LNG facilities from its joint venture with QatarEnergy represent a hit of about 3% of global production, with a repair time of “between 3 and 5 years.” This long-duration disruption suggests the old drawdown patterns remain a relevant guide to the risk. Can you ride out a fall of that magnitude? That deepest 48% drawdown would have cut about 5% from your whole portfolio if Exxon Mobil was a 10% position. While media releases or rumors about a substantial change in a company's business prospects usually make its stock 'trending' and lead to an immediate price change, there are always some fundamental facts that eventually dominate the buy-and-hold decision-making. Here at Zacks, we prioritize appraising the change in the projection of a company's future earnings over anything else. That's because we believe the present value of its future stream of earnings is what determines the fair value for its stock. Our analysis is essentially based on how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to take the latest business trends into account. When earnings estimates for a company go up, the fair value for its stock goes up as well. And when a stock's fair value is higher than its current market price, investors tend to buy the stock, resulting in its price moving upward. Because of this, empirical studies indicate a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and short-term stock price movements. Exxon is expected to post earnings of $3.96 per share for the current quarter, representing a year-over-year change of +141.5%. Over the last 30 days, the Zacks Consensus Estimate has changed +2.9%. For the next fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $10.66 indicates a change of -10.1% from what Exxon is expected to report a year ago. Over the past month, the estimate has changed +0.5%. With an impressive externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool -- the Zacks Rank -- is a more conclusive indicator of a stock's near-term price performance, as it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions. The size of the recent change in the consensus estimate, along with three other factors related to earnings estimates, has resulted in a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) for Exxon. It's almost impossible for a company to grow its earnings without growing its revenue for long periods. Therefore, knowing a company's potential revenue growth is crucial. Compared to the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $81.49 billion, the reported revenues represent a surprise of +4.47%. The EPS surprise was +8.41%.                                        My Trusted Source Integrated energy company Exxon Mobil manages worldwide production, refining, and chemical operations while maintaining significant representation within the S&P 500 Index . The energy sector plays a central role in global economic activity, supplying fuels, lubricants, petrochemicals, and other products that support transportation, manufacturing, and industrial operations. Within this sector, Exxon Mobil (NYSE:XOM) is one of the world's largest integrated energy companies. As a major constituent of the S&P 500 Index , the company participates in exploration, production, refining, chemicals, and energy-related technologies across numerous regions. Exxon Mobil operates through a diversified business model that spans multiple parts of the energy value chain. Activities begin with the exploration and production of crude oil and natural gas in several geographic markets, including North America, South America, Asia-Pacific, Europe, the Middle East, and Africa. The company also manages refining operations that convert crude oil into transportation fuels and other petroleum products. These facilities supply gasoline, diesel, aviation fuels, lubricants, and specialty products used throughout industrial and consumer markets. Chemical manufacturing represents another major component of operations. Petrochemical facilities produce materials utilized in packaging, automotive manufacturing, construction, healthcare applications, and consumer goods. The company is frequently discussed alongside Energy Stocks due to its scale and broad operational footprint. Integrated energy producers occupy a distinct position within the sector because they participate in both resource extraction and product manufacturing. This structure differentiates integrated companies from pure exploration firms or standalone refiners. Market conditions affecting crude oil, natural gas, refined products, and petrochemicals can influence various segments differently, creating a diversified operational profile. Within the broader energy industry, Exxon Mobil (NYSE:XOM) maintains assets that support production, transportation, processing, and distribution activities across multiple continents. Exploration and production activities remain a significant element of company operations. Upstream assets include offshore developments, conventional fields, shale resources, and natural gas projects. Major producing regions include the Permian Basin in the United States, offshore Guyana developments, and projects located across several international markets. Production volumes are supported by ongoing drilling programs, infrastructure development, and resource management initiatives. Natural gas continues to represent an important component of operations as global demand for cleaner-burning fuel sources remains a notable industry trend. Liquefied natural gas projects also contribute to international energy supply networks. Refining operations form an essential connection between crude production and end-user consumption. Facilities process raw hydrocarbons into fuels and specialty products used throughout transportation, industrial manufacturing, and commercial activities. Global refining networks enable the company to supply products to domestic and international markets. Operational efficiency, maintenance activities, logistics management, and product demand patterns influence refinery performance. Petrochemical manufacturing further expands the business beyond transportation fuels. Chemical products support industries ranging from healthcare and electronics to packaging and construction materials. Global energy demand continues to be influenced by population growth, industrial development, urbanization, and expanding transportation requirements. These trends affect demand patterns for crude oil, natural gas, fuels, and petrochemical products. Energy producers also operate within an environment shaped by technological advancement, emissions-reduction initiatives, and infrastructure modernization. Developments in carbon capture, lower-emission fuels, and operational efficiency have become increasingly relevant throughout the industry. As a large integrated operator, Exxon Mobil participates in several initiatives connected to industrial emissions management, carbon capture technologies, and energy infrastructure development. Operations extend across numerous countries and regions, providing exposure to a diverse range of resource basins and customer markets. Production assets, refining facilities, chemical plants, and distribution networks contribute to a broad international footprint. Guyana has emerged as a notable area of activity due to significant offshore discoveries and ongoing project development. In North America, the Permian Basin remains a key production region supported by extensive infrastructure and operational capabilities. Additional assets across Europe, Asia-Pacific, Africa, and South America contribute to global production and product distribution activities. The global energy industry remains influenced by commodity supply trends, transportation networks, refining capacity, and changing consumption patterns. Geopolitical developments, shipping routes, and infrastructure availability can affect market conditions throughout the sector. Integrated producers must coordinate production activities with refining operations and product distribution systems. This requires extensive logistical planning, technical expertise, and asset management across multiple jurisdictions. The company's scale enables participation in various segments of the energy ecosystem, ranging from upstream resource development to downstream manufacturing and marketing activities. The energy sector remains an important component of the U.S. equity market, and large integrated companies frequently attract attention due to their operational scale and global reach. Within this context, Exxon Mobil (NYSE:XOM) remains a significant participant in the S&P 500 Index and the broader energy industry. Its combination of upstream production, refining operations, chemical manufacturing capabilities, and international asset portfolio reflects the characteristics commonly associated with large integrated energy enterprises. Ongoing developments in energy demand, infrastructure expansion, resource development, and industrial technologies continue to shape the operating environment for major companies throughout the sector, including participants within the S&P 500 Index .
